scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Dominican dance bands such as the Casimir Brothers and The Swinging Stars had provided dance music across the island through the 1940s and 1950s.
Calypso and steelpan gained ascendancy in Roseau during the 1960s, while Haitian musicians introduced cadence rampa (méringue) across the French Antilles and Dominica.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The music and dance served as both popular recreational dancehall entertainment and a political vehicle for nationalist ferment, anti-colonial protest, and conscious-raising in post-colonial Dominica.

It bridged generations, linking older listeners familiar with accordion-driven jing ping folk traditions with youth embracing Black Power consciousness, while also offering early platforms for social commentary on women's issues through artists like Ophelia Marie.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Cadence-lypso music combines Haitian cadence rampa and Trinidadian calypso with United States funk bass, soul-style vocals, and rock guitars influenced by Carlos Santana and Osibisa.
Keyboards, horn sections, percussive instruments, and newly introduced synthesizers formed the instrumental bedrock.
Listen for the synthesizer, horns, electric guitar, bass guitar.

A high-energy Creole dance groove characterized by driving funk basslines, rock-inflected guitar chords, bright brass horn arrangements, and rhythmic synthesizers underneath expressive soul-influenced vocals delivered in Dominican French Creole.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Cadence-lypso thrived in commercial dance clubs, school dances, dance halls, and open-air festival spaces such as Roseau's Newtown Savannah.
Overseas, Dominican performers played iconic Parisian venues including the Théâtre Noir, Cirque d'Hiver, and Théâtre de la Renaissance.
Visual aesthetics and community style reflected the 1970s Black Power and Rastafarian movements, emphasizing Black identity, pro-African pride, and contemporary popular fashion.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Gordon Henderson, leader of Exile One, coined the term cadence-lypso and defined its framework.
Other leading vocalists and musicians included Jeff Joseph, Marcel 'Chubby' Marc, Anthony Gussie, Mike Moreau, Tony Valmond, Linford John, Bill Thomas, Sinky Rabess, and Janet Azouz.

Originating in Dominica and developed by Dominican musicians based in Guadeloupe, cadence-lypso developed strong followings and performance circuits in Martinique, Haiti, France, Latin America, and parts of Africa, adapting to varied club scenes across the Francophone and Anglophone Caribbean.
Cadence-lypso descends directly from Haitian cadence rampa, Trinidadian calypso, and Dominican folk forms like jing ping, alongside 1960s American soul and funk.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Cadence-lypso is parent of cadence rampa: Haitian cadence rampa forms the structural rhythmic basis for cadence-lypso.
Cadence-lypso is parent of calypso: Trinidadian calypso provided vital beats and melodic phrasing that Exile One synthesized into the style.
Cadence-lypso is child of zouk: Cadence-lypso was instrumental in the late-20th-century evolution of French Antillean zouk.
Cadence-lypso is child of soca: The cross-pollination of cadence-lypso contributed to the development of modern soca music.
